title: Promises before the wedding
subtitle: Nuptial agreements, Radmacher and the push for reform
objectives: Explain why a pre- or post-nuptial agreement is a factor within s 25, not an automatic bar to the court's discretion
State the three Radmacher conditions for giving an agreement decisive weight and apply them to a new fact pattern
Describe the government's live proposal for statutorily binding 'qualifying nuptial agreements' and explain why it is not yet law

leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that a freely entered nuptial agreement, made with full appreciation of its implications, should be given effect unless it would be unfair to hold the parties to it in the circumstances prevailing

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can say 'prenups aren't automatically binding in England' — that's the easy half. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know agreements aren't a veto — this lesson is about running the Radmacher conditions on facts where the answer genuinely could go either way.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans hard on scenario questions built around the three Radmacher conditions — expect to weigh disclosure, legal advice, timing and later circumstances against each other, not just recite the test.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state why an agreement is a factor rather than a bar before moving on — the rest of this lesson assumes that starting point.

overview.hook: England and Wales has never had a clean rule that a signed prenup is binding, full stop. Instead it has a doctrine built out of one landmark case, a discretion that can override even a carefully drafted agreement, and — as of this year — a live government proposal that would, for the first time, make some agreements genuinely binding by statute. This lesson teaches the law as it stands today, and is honest about the line between that law and where it might be heading.
overview.lawStatedNotice: The Radmacher test below is settled, current law. The proposal for statutorily binding 'qualifying nuptial agreements', covered in Part 5, is a live government policy proposal only: the consultation on wider financial remedies reform (which includes this proposal) closed on 14 August 2026, the government was still analysing responses as at the date this lesson was written, and no legislation implementing qualifying nuptial agreements has been introduced. Students must not treat qualifying nuptial agreements as current law. Law stated as at 24 September 2026.

parts.heading: A factor, not a veto
parts.voice: argumentative — states the older orthodoxy, then complicates it
body: For most of the twentieth century, English courts treated agreements about what should happen to money on divorce with real suspicion — even outright hostility. The reasoning was rooted in public policy: parties should not be free to contract out of the court's statutory jurisdiction over financial remedies, and an agreement signed before a marriage even began, when both parties were (in theory) optimistic about its permanence, was an unreliable guide to what fairness required years later.

That hostility has substantially softened, but the underlying statutory position has not changed: a nuptial agreement — whether pre-nuptial (signed before the wedding) or post-nuptial (signed afterwards) — is not a contract the court is bound to enforce. The court's jurisdiction under s 25 MCA 1973 cannot be ousted by private agreement. What has changed is how much weight an agreement is given within that discretion.

It is easy to state this half of the doctrine and stop there, which is exactly the trap this lesson is built to catch: 'prenups aren't binding in England' is true as a headline and useless as an answer, because the real content of the law is in how much weight an agreement gets — and that is governed almost entirely by one 2010 Supreme Court decision.

components.definition: A pre-nuptial agreement (signed before marriage) or post-nuptial agreement (signed after) setting out how the parties intend their finances to be divided if the marriage ends. Neither type ousts the court's s 25 jurisdiction, but both can be given decisive weight within it.

interaction.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the legal status of a validly signed pre-nuptial agreement in England and Wales?
options: It automatically binds the court, ousting its discretion under s 25
It has no legal effect whatsoever and the court must ignore it entirely
It is a factor the court takes into account under its s 25 discretion, capable of being given decisive weight but not automatically binding
interaction.trapExplanation: Both extremes are wrong. A prenup cannot oust the court's statutory jurisdiction (so it isn't automatically binding), but courts have moved a long way from ignoring agreements altogether — since Radmacher, a properly made agreement can be given decisive, effectively determinative weight.

parts.heading: Radmacher v Granatino: the facts
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Katrin Radmacher, a wealthy German heiress, and Nicolas Granatino, a French investment banker, signed a prenuptial agreement in Germany before their marriage, providing that neither would make a claim on the other's assets if the marriage ended. Ms Radmacher's family wanted to protect substantial family wealth; Mr Granatino took independent legal advice in France, though he declined the opportunity for full financial disclosure of his fiancée's wealth, understanding in general terms that she was very rich.

The marriage broke down after roughly eight years, by which point Mr Granatino had left investment banking for a lower-paid academic career, partly to support the family. At first instance he was awarded a substantial sum, disregarding the agreement's terms as unfair. The Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court took a very different view of how much weight the agreement should carry.

The Supreme Court held that the agreement should be given decisive weight, sharply reducing Mr Granatino's award compared with what he might otherwise have received, while still making some provision for the children's needs. The case is now the foundational modern authority on how nuptial agreements are treated in England and Wales.

components.factsShort: Wealthy heiress and investment banker sign a prenuptial agreement excluding claims on each other's assets; the marriage ends after eight years, by which time the husband has left banking for lower-paid academic work.
components.ratioShort: The court should give effect to a nuptial agreement freely entered into by each party with a full appreciation of its implications, unless in the circumstances prevailing it would not be fair to hold the parties to it.

expanded.facts: Ms Radmacher and Mr Granatino signed a prenuptial agreement in Germany excluding financial claims on divorce, primarily to protect Ms Radmacher's family wealth. Mr Granatino received independent legal advice but waived full disclosure of the extent of his fiancée's assets. Years later, after the marriage broke down, he sought a financial award well beyond what the agreement contemplated, arguing it should carry little or no weight.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The majority held: 'The court should give effect to a nuptial agreement that is freely entered into by each party with a full appreciation of its implications unless in the circumstances prevailing it would not be fair to hold the parties to their agreement.' The Court also held that agreements cannot be used to prejudice the reasonable requirements of any children of the family, whatever their terms otherwise provide.
expanded.significance: Radmacher transformed the practical status of nuptial agreements in England and Wales. Without changing the formal legal position — an agreement still cannot oust the court's jurisdiction — it created a structured test under which a properly made agreement will, in most cases, be decisive, reversing the earlier practice of treating such agreements as of marginal relevance.

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened in Radmacher v Granatino.
items: The parties sign a prenuptial agreement before marrying, excluding claims on each other's assets
They marry and, over the following years, Mr Granatino leaves investment banking for lower-paid academic work
The marriage breaks down and Mr Granatino seeks an award well beyond the agreement's terms
The Supreme Court gives the agreement decisive weight, sharply reducing his award
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the arc: agreement, marriage and career change, breakdown, and then the Supreme Court's decision to hold the parties broadly to what they had agreed in advance.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the agreement is signed before the wedding, the career change happens during the marriage, the claim for more than the agreement provided comes on breakdown, and the Supreme Court's ruling giving the agreement decisive weight comes last.

parts.heading: The three Radmacher conditions
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Radmacher doesn't say every agreement will be upheld — it sets a structured test for deciding how much weight to give one. Three conditions matter most: free entry into the agreement, a full appreciation of its implications, and fairness in the circumstances prevailing at the time the court is asked to enforce it.

Free entry asks whether the agreement was signed voluntarily, without undue pressure — signing under a threat, or being presented with an agreement to sign the day before the wedding with no realistic option to walk away, undermines this condition. Full appreciation of implications asks whether each party understood, in broad terms, what they were giving up — this is where independent legal advice and reasonably adequate financial disclosure do real work, though Radmacher itself shows that disclosure can be waived if the general picture is understood.

The third condition — fairness in the circumstances prevailing — is the one that keeps the court's discretion alive even for a well-made agreement. Even a freely entered, fully understood agreement will not be enforced if holding the parties to it would be unfair given how things actually turned out, and Radmacher was explicit that an agreement can never be used to leave a party without provision for their needs, and can never prejudice the reasonable requirements of any children.

components.label: The three Radmacher conditions
points: Free entry — no undue pressure, duress, or a fait accompli sprung on one party shortly before the wedding

Full appreciation of implications — each party broadly understood what they were agreeing to, typically evidenced by independent legal advice and adequate (though not necessarily exhaustive) financial disclosure

Fairness in the circumstances prevailing — an agreement will not be enforced where doing so would be unfair given how matters have actually turned out, and can never leave a party without provision for needs or prejudice the reasonable requirements of any children
An agreement meeting all three conditions is normally given decisive weight, but the court's discretion is never wholly excluded

interaction.prompt: Two weeks before their wedding, with invitations sent and the venue booked, Leo's fiancée presents him with a prenuptial agreement drafted by her family's solicitors and tells him the wedding is off unless he signs it immediately, with no time to take his own legal advice. Which Radmacher condition is most clearly undermined?
options: Free entry — the timing and pressure make this look far from voluntary
Full appreciation of implications only — free entry is not in issue here
Fairness in the circumstances prevailing — the other two conditions are clearly satisfied
interaction.explanation: This is a textbook challenge to free entry: presenting an agreement at the last minute, with an ultimatum and no time for independent advice, is exactly the kind of pressure that undermines voluntariness, whatever the agreement's terms actually say.

parts.heading: When fairness overrides a well-made agreement
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the hard case before resolving it
body: Suppose an agreement passes both the free-entry and full-appreciation conditions cleanly — properly advised, disclosed, signed months in advance with no pressure. Can it still be set aside? Yes, and this is the part of Radmacher students most often underweight: the third condition, fairness in the circumstances prevailing, operates even then.

The clearest example is needs. However clearly an agreement excludes financial claims, it cannot be used to leave a party — or, especially, children of the family — without adequate provision. An agreement signed by two wealthy professionals with no children, years before either developed a disability or gave up a career, may look very different in its fairness once actually applied to a marriage that produced three children and a decade of one party out of the workforce.

The court is, in effect, asking two different questions that can pull in different directions: was this agreement fairly made, and would it be fair to hold the parties to it now? An agreement can pass the first test comprehensively and still fail the second, because circumstances at the time of enforcement — not just at the time of signing — are what fairness in the circumstances prevailing actually measures.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that once an agreement is shown to be freely entered with full disclosure and independent advice, it is automatically enforced in full.
components.whyItsWrong: Radmacher's third condition survives even a well-made agreement. Fairness is assessed against the circumstances prevailing at the time enforcement is sought, not only at signing — needs, especially of children, can never be sacrificed to an agreement, however cleanly it was made.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is a well-made prenuptial agreement most likely to be overridden on fairness grounds, despite satisfying free entry and full appreciation?
interaction.scenarioA: A short, childless marriage between two financially independent professionals, both of whom remain in broadly the same financial position at separation as when they signed the agreement.
interaction.scenarioB: A fifteen-year marriage that has produced three children; one spouse gave up a career to care for them and, without provision beyond the agreement's terms, would be left unable to house the children adequately.
interaction.explanation: B is the paradigm case for overriding even a well-made agreement: the agreement, however fairly signed, cannot be used to leave children without adequate housing or a caring parent without basic provision — that is the needs floor Radmacher preserves regardless of how the agreement was made.

parts.heading: A live proposal: qualifying nuptial agreements
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by locating the current debate
body: Radmacher created a strong practical presumption in favour of enforcing well-made agreements, but it stopped short of making them automatically binding by law — the court's discretion, and the needs floor, remain in place regardless of how carefully an agreement is drafted. Some practitioners and reform bodies have long argued this leaves too much uncertainty for couples who want genuine certainty about their financial position.

As part of a wider package of financial remedies reform, the government has been consulting on introducing statutorily binding 'qualifying nuptial agreements' — agreements that, if they met defined statutory safeguards (broadly tracking the Radmacher conditions: independent advice, financial disclosure, no undue pressure, and protection for needs), would be enforceable as a matter of law rather than merely given strong weight within a continuing judicial discretion.

This is genuinely unsettled ground. The consultation closed on 14 August 2026, and as at the date this lesson was written the government was still analysing responses, with no Bill introduced and no implementation timetable published. Students should be able to describe the proposal and explain why it would change the law if enacted — but must not describe qualifying nuptial agreements as though they already exist. The current, operative law remains the discretionary Radmacher test taught in Parts 2 to 4 of this lesson.

components.definition: A proposed statutory category of nuptial agreement that, if it met defined safeguards echoing the Radmacher conditions, would be automatically binding rather than merely a weighty factor within the court's s 25 discretion. This is a live policy proposal, not current law, as at the date this lesson was written.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that statutorily binding qualifying nuptial agreements are currently the law in England and Wales?
interaction.explanation: Not yet law. Qualifying nuptial agreements remain a live government policy proposal: the relevant consultation closed on 14 August 2026 with the outcome not yet published, and no legislation has been introduced. The operative law today is still the discretionary Radmacher test.

testPool.prompt: Name the case that established the modern test for how much weight a nuptial agreement should be given.
Name the three conditions from Radmacher relevant to how much weight a nuptial agreement is given.
acceptableAnswers: free entry, full appreciation of implications, fairness in the circumstances prevailing
testPool.modelAnswer: Free entry into the agreement, full appreciation of its implications, and fairness in the circumstances prevailing.

testPool.prompt: Can a pre-nuptial agreement, however carefully made, oust the court's statutory jurisdiction under s 25 MCA 1973?
options: No — it remains a factor within the court's discretion, even if a very weighty one
Yes — a properly made agreement removes the court's jurisdiction entirely
testPool.explanation: Radmacher did not change the formal legal position that s 25 jurisdiction cannot be ousted by private agreement. What it changed is how much weight a properly made agreement is given within that jurisdiction — up to and including decisive weight.

testPool.prompt: According to Radmacher, can a nuptial agreement be used to leave the children of the family without adequate provision?
options: No — an agreement can never prejudice the reasonable requirements of any children
Yes — if both parents signed the agreement, it binds the children's provision too
testPool.explanation: Radmacher was explicit that whatever weight an agreement is given between the spouses, it cannot be used to leave the children of the family without adequate provision.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most directly undermines the 'full appreciation of implications' condition.
testPool.scenarioText: Nadia and Piotr sign a prenuptial agreement four months before their wedding. Nadia takes independent legal advice from a family solicitor. Piotr refuses any legal advice, is not shown any figures for Nadia's assets, and signs the document without asking what it means, believing it to be a formality.
tappableSpans: is not shown any figures for Nadia's assets
testPool.correctSpan: is not shown any figures for Nadia's assets
testPool.explanation: Refusing advice alone might not be fatal if Piotr otherwise understood the position, but combined with being given no figures at all and believing the document to be a mere formality, the lack of any disclosure is what most clearly undermines his full appreciation of what he was agreeing to.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most directly engages the 'fairness in the circumstances prevailing' condition, rather than free entry or full appreciation.
testPool.scenarioText: Tom and Julia signed a comprehensive prenuptial agreement eight months before their wedding, both independently advised, with full financial disclosure on each side. Fifteen years later, after Julia developed a severe long-term disability during the marriage that ended her ability to work, the agreement as written would leave her with no housing and no income.
tappableSpans: signed a comprehensive prenuptial agreement eight months before their wedding
both independently advised, with full financial disclosure
developed a severe long-term disability during the marriage
would leave her with no housing and no income
testPool.correctSpan: would leave her with no housing and no income
testPool.explanation: The first two conditions are plainly satisfied here — the problem is fairness at the point of enforcement. An agreement that would leave a spouse with no housing and no income engages the needs floor Radmacher preserves, regardless of how properly the agreement was made at signing.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between the three Radmacher conditions?
options: All three must fail before a court will decline to enforce an agreement
An agreement can satisfy free entry and full appreciation of implications and still be refused effect on fairness grounds
Fairness in the circumstances prevailing only applies to post-nuptial, not pre-nuptial, agreements
testPool.trapExplanation: The conditions are not cumulative hurdles that all have to fail together — fairness in the circumstances prevailing operates independently, and can override an agreement that was, in every other respect, freely and knowingly made. Radmacher applies its full test to both pre- and post-nuptial agreements.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following most accurately reflects the Radmacher test for giving a nuptial agreement decisive weight?
options: The court should give effect to an agreement freely entered into with full appreciation of its implications, unless it would not be fair to hold the parties to it in the circumstances prevailing
The court must enforce any signed agreement regardless of the circumstances at the time of divorce
The court should disregard nuptial agreements entirely and decide the case solely on the ordinary s 25 factors
testPool.explanation: This is close to the Supreme Court's own formulation in Radmacher: an agreement freely made with full appreciation of its implications should be given effect, unless fairness in the circumstances prevailing at enforcement points the other way.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court works through when deciding how much weight to give a nuptial agreement.
items: Establish the terms of the agreement and when it was signed
Assess whether it was freely entered without undue pressure
Assess whether each party had a full appreciation of its implications
Assess whether it would be fair to hold the parties to it in the circumstances now prevailing

testPool.prompt: In which scenario is a nuptial agreement most likely to be given decisive weight under Radmacher?
testPool.scenarioA: A post-nuptial agreement signed by both spouses, each independently advised, with full disclosure, reviewed and re-confirmed ten years into a marriage that produced no children, where both parties remain financially independent at separation.
testPool.scenarioB: A pre-nuptial agreement signed the night before the wedding, with no legal advice offered to one party, presented as a condition of the wedding proceeding at all.
testPool.explanation: A satisfies all three Radmacher conditions comfortably: free entry, full appreciation through independent advice and disclosure, and fairness in circumstances that have not materially changed. B fails on free entry alone — the timing and the ultimatum are exactly the kind of pressure Radmacher treats as undermining voluntariness.

testPool.prompt: A couple sign a post-nuptial agreement two years into their marriage, both independently advised and with full disclosure, agreeing to keep their finances entirely separate. They divorce twelve years later with no children and both remaining financially independent throughout. What weight is the agreement likely to be given?
options: Decisive weight — all three Radmacher conditions appear satisfied and nothing suggests it would now be unfair to hold the parties to it
No weight — post-nuptial agreements are treated far more sceptically than pre-nuptial agreements
Decisive weight only if the agreement was re-signed every five years
testPool.explanation: Radmacher applies the same structured test to post-nuptial agreements as to pre-nuptial ones. With free entry, full appreciation and no change in circumstances pointing towards unfairness, this agreement is a strong candidate for decisive weight.

testPool.prompt: Six months before their wedding, Farrah and Ollie sign a prenuptial agreement excluding claims on each other's pre-marital assets. Both take independent legal advice and exchange full financial disclosure. Twenty years and two children later, Ollie — who gave up a well-paid career to raise the children at Farrah's request — would, under the agreement's strict terms, receive nothing beyond basic child maintenance and would be unable to rehouse himself or the children. Analyse how the court is likely to treat the agreement.
factsToOrder: The agreement was signed six months before the wedding with independent advice and full disclosure on both sides
The marriage lasted twenty years and produced two children
Ollie gave up a well-paid career at Farrah's request to raise the children
Under the agreement's strict terms, Ollie would be unable to rehouse himself or the children

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion

No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a prenuptial agreement that was freely made and fully understood at signing should nonetheless be departed from because enforcing it in full would leave a spouse and children without adequate housing.
modelAnswer.rule: Radmacher v Granatino requires effect to be given to an agreement freely entered into with full appreciation of its implications, unless it would not be fair to hold the parties to it in the circumstances prevailing; an agreement can never prejudice the reasonable requirements of any children of the family, and needs are never fully excluded by an agreement.
modelAnswer.application: Free entry and full appreciation are both comfortably satisfied here — independent advice, full disclosure, six months before the wedding. The live issue is the third condition. Twenty years on, with two children and a spouse who sacrificed his own earning capacity at the other party's request, strict enforcement of the agreement would leave Ollie and the children without housing — precisely the outcome Radmacher rules out, regardless of how properly the agreement was made.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The agreement is likely to be given weight as to the general principle of separating pre-marital wealth, but the court will depart from its strict terms to the extent necessary to meet Ollie's and the children's needs, most likely through a housing-focused award funded from Farrah's resources.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a nuptial agreement, once shown to satisfy free entry and full appreciation of implications, is always enforced in full regardless of later circumstances?
testPool.explanation: Not always. Radmacher's third condition — fairness in the circumstances prevailing — can still override an agreement that was properly made, particularly where enforcing it in full would leave a party or the children without adequate provision.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below drawn from the Radmacher judgment, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: Parties are free to enter into whatever agreements they wish, but a court is not bound to give effect to such agreements as if they were contracts in the ordinary sense. The court should give effect to a nuptial agreement that is freely entered into by each party with a full appreciation of its implications unless in the circumstances prevailing it would not be fair to hold the parties to their agreement.
testPool.ratioSentence: The court should give effect to a nuptial agreement that is freely entered into by each party with a full appreciation of its implications unless in the circumstances prevailing it would not be fair to hold the parties to their agreement.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating an agreement's fairness at signing as the end of the analysis, and treating the proposed 'qualifying nuptial agreement' reform as though it were already in force. Both mistakes collapse a live discretion, or a live policy debate, into a settled rule that doesn't yet exist.
